extracted.intended_audience: aspiring authors, poets, and literary practitioners considering publication or composition
extracted.subtask_short: writing and publishing advice for authors
extracted.subtask_description: Practical and aesthetic guidance for authors on publishing strategies (subscriptions vs trade, finances, dealings with booksellers/printers) and on compositional choices for long poems (subject unity, transitions, use of observation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer selling copyright to self-publishing
rubrics_metrics.description: The most prudent mode is to sell the copyright, at least of one or more editions, for the most that the trade will offer; fifty pounds and ease of mind are of more real advantage than the chance of five hundred with the certainty of insult and degrading anxieties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: selling copyright transfers financial risk and worry to the trade; authors should accept modest payment for security. Example/advice: do not attempt to unite the functions of author and publisher; accept that few authors will gain a large remuneration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid uniting author and publisher
rubrics_metrics.description: It is better not to attempt in any way to unite the functions of author and publisher.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: combining roles increases costs (paper, printing) and administrative burdens; the trade exists for a reason. Practical implication: prefer trade publication or selling copyright rather than running publishing operations yourself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subscription/self-publishing by post is risky and often impractical
rubrics_metrics.description: Publishing by subscription and sending works by post involves pre-buying stamped paper, considerable postage costs, delayed receipt of subscription money, and many subscribers dropping out without notice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence: many subscribers dropped before paying; postage and stocking paper can erase expected margins; anecdote of an Earl who kept issues but never paid. Implication: factor in postal delays/costs and unreliable subscribers if choosing this route.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manage finances and expectations with printers/publishers
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors should not expect printers or booksellers to wait indefinitely for payment; delays and slow receipts can lead to severe financial consequences including the threat of imprisonment for unpaid printing bills.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: author nearly thrown into jail by Bristol printer who refused to wait for a month for £80–90; practical advice: secure funds or a guarantor before printing; avoid overextending credit with tradesmen.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be honest and reliable about publication dates
rubrics_metrics.description: Delaying publication beyond the announced day harms subscriber trust and can cause subscribers to abandon the work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: publication of the first number of The Watchman was delayed and the second number's controversial essay then lost near five hundred subscribers. Practical rule: meet announced dates or expect reputational/financial loss.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose a subject that supplies unity for a long poem
rubrics_metrics.description: Select a subject that gives equal room for description, incident, and impassioned reflections and that supplies a natural connection among parts so as to yield unity to the whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critique/example: The Task was judged defective because its title-subject could not be carried beyond a few pages and connections were often awkward; the author planned The Brook as a stream traced from source to sea to secure organic unity across episodes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain coherent transitions and connections in extended composition
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid frequent awkward connections and abrupt, arbitrary transitions within a long poem or extended work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critical note: abrupt transitions reduce unity and reader comprehension. Practical method: choose a binding subject or narrative thread to smooth transitions and justify digressions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be audience-aware: political or religious positions affect readership
rubrics_metrics.description: Publishing opinions on hot political or religious topics can rapidly alienate subscribers and supporters; a single controversial essay may lose hundreds of readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: an essay against fast days with a censurable use of Isaiah's text lost near 500 subscribers at once. Practical implication: weigh the costs of speaking freely on contentious matters if you depend on subscriptions or a particular constituency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer canvassing by proxy rather than in-person solicitation
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors are advised to avoid repeated personal canvassing for subscribers; canvass by proxy (friends/introducers) to secure subscriptions more acceptably.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence: personal canvass efforts met with ridicule or refusal; friends recommended canvass by proxy after hospitable receptions but persuasive discouragement to continue personal solicitation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Work from direct observation and field studies in composing descriptive poetry
rubrics_metrics.description: Make on-site studies (sketches/notebooks) and craft verse with the objects and imagery immediately before the senses to supply authentic description and material for composition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practice: walk the landscape (e.g., Quantock), use pencil and memorandum-book to record studies, and mould thoughts into verse informed by immediate observation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency of principle is safer than partial dissent in public life
rubrics_metrics.description: A person who opposes a political or religious zealot entirely is generally safer from their obloquy than one who differs only in degree or in one or two points.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implication for authors: inconsistent or moderate positions may attract more hostility than clear opposition; consider how consistently you present your views to avoid misinterpretation or intensified partisan attack.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not vilify tradesmen for systemic trade practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors should avoid speaking unkindly or opprobriously of booksellers or tradesmen as individuals, since they do not make the laws and customs of their trade.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Moral admonition: complain only if the underlying evil can be shown removable without greater inconvenience; otherwise it is unwise and immoral to calumniate individuals for systemic practices.
